format_overrides.narrative_mode: An external lore narrator tells the canonical item's history in third person. The item never speaks as I or me. Do not invent sentience or agency unless canon establishes it.
format_overrides.visual_priority: The item is the largest and sharpest focal subject in every clip. Owners appear as hands, torso crops, silhouettes, or secondary figures unless identity is necessary to understand the event.
format_overrides.structure: HOOK (the recovered sword corrupts Worf and Kor) → MYTHIC ORIGIN → LEGENDARY PURPOSE → HUR'Q THEFT / LOST MILLENNIUM → RECOVERY → CHOICE / FATE IN SPACE → CTA
format_overrides.era_prompt_rule: Do not use TOS, TNG, DS9, or other era abbreviations in image/video prompts. Describe uniform cuts and colors explicitly.
format_overrides.state_continuity: The Sword remains physically intact throughout this episode. Age is shown through surface patina and environment, not silhouette redesign. Its dense pale wavy etching and unique four-horn profile must remain unchanged in every post-forging scene.

voice_policy.intent: low resonant masculine lore narrator, measured and grave, controlled Klingon ceremonial weight, never shouting, never a direct imitation of a canon actor
voice_policy.note: The narrator speaks about the sword in third person. The sword is not canonically sentient. Do not use a character voice clone.

items.category: the first Klingon bat'leth and sacred cultural artifact
items.canon_scope: Prime-timeline television canon only. Do not import Star Trek Online, novels, comics, Memory Beta, or other licensed-game continuation events.

appearance_lock.overall_shape: Approximately 1.4 meters wide, horizontally symmetrical double-ended bat'leth with a shallow crescent body. Four unmistakable upward/outward horn points define the silhouette: two long spear-like outer tips and two tall inward-curving blade horns rising near the inner thirds. The lower edge forms a broad central downward crescent around the grip area, with three hand positions/openings integrated into the blade.
appearance_lock.material: Dark charcoal gunmetal steel with slightly brighter sharpened edges; dense pale silver-gray flowing wavy patterning covers almost the entire blade surface like layered Damascus steel. Ancient and subtly weathered but intact, never rusty, chipped, broken, glowing, or magical.
appearance_lock.grips: Three dark wrapped hand grips integrated along the lower central span; practical two-handed scale. No conventional sword hilt, crossguard, pommel, scabbard, chain, jewels, gold trim, or separate handle.
appearance_lock.surface_details: The pale pattern is irregular, fine, and organic across every blade section. Do not replace it with large readable Klingon letters, neon runes, engraved text, Celtic knots, flames, or generic fantasy filigree.
appearance_lock.scale_lock: When held horizontally, the weapon spans roughly from beyond one adult shoulder to beyond the other. Hands occupy the central grips; the blade remains too wide to be mistaken for a knife, sword, mek'leth, or standard smooth bat'leth.
appearance_lock.negative_lock: No generic smooth bat'leth, no single-edged saber, no katana, no medieval longsword, no axe, no double-headed axe, no fantasy glowing weapon, no gold ornament, no red blade, no blue energy, no readable lettering, no extra spikes, no missing inner horns, no asymmetry.

item_states.appearance: The recognizable four-horn bat'leth silhouette has just formed from dark incandescent metal-like material; edges retain a restrained orange heat while the pale wavy surface pattern begins to emerge. This is a visualization of Klingon legend, not a scientific reconstruction.

The exact canonical DS9 artifact: dark charcoal gunmetal, pale dense wavy pattern over the whole blade, brighter edges, three dark grips, four-horn symmetrical silhouette, ancient patina but structurally intact.

canonical_facts.fact: Klingon tradition identifies it as the first bat'leth, forged by Kahless the Unforgettable.
canonical_facts.source: TNG: Rightful Heir; DS9: The Sword of Kahless

canonical_facts.fact: The origin story says Kahless placed a lock of his hair into lava from Kri'stak and cooled it in the Lake of Lusor before shaping the blade.
canonical_facts.status: Klingon mythology; narration must label it as legend

canonical_facts.fact: The Hur'q stole the Sword during their invasion and plunder of Qo'noS; it remained missing for roughly a millennium.
Kor, Worf, and Jadzia Dax recovered it from a Hur'q site in the Gamma Quadrant in 2372.
Its symbolic power drove Worf and Kor into a violent struggle over who should wield it and lead the Klingon people.
canonical_facts.status: television canon; do not claim confirmed supernatural mind control

canonical_facts.fact: They concluded the Sword would divide the Empire and transported it into interstellar space, where television canon leaves it drifting.

forbidden_claims: The Sword is literally sentient or speaks in canon.
The Sword has confirmed supernatural mind-control powers.
The Sword was recovered after Worf, Kor, and Dax left it in space in television canon.
Star Trek Online's later Hur'q, Martok, Kahless II, J'mpok, Aakar, or L'Rell events belong to television canon.
The blade is made from Hur'q carapace or germanium; that is licensed-game continuity, not the DS9 television story.

items.category: a hand-carved wooden flute from a dead civilization, kept by Picard as the only physical trace of a lifetime he never actually lived
items.canon_scope: Prime-timeline television canon only (TNG: The Inner Light). Do not import novels, comics, Memory Beta, or other licensed continuation events.

appearance_lock.overall_shape: A slender straight wooden flute, roughly 35-40cm long, simple cylindrical body of consistent diameter along its length, tapering slightly at the mouth end. Six evenly-spaced round finger holes along the top, one embouchure hole near one end, open bore visible at both ends. No bell, no keys, no valves, no metal mechanism of any kind.
appearance_lock.material: Warm honey-brown natural wood with visible fine grain lines running lengthwise, hand-sanded matte-satin surface. No lacquer shine, no metal bands, no inlay, no paint.
appearance_lock.grips: No separate grip or handle; the player's fingers rest directly over the finger holes along the plain cylindrical body.
appearance_lock.surface_details: A few faint hand-worn polish marks near the finger holes from decades of playing. No carvings, no engraved script, no painted decoration, no attached cord or strap, no gemstones or metal fittings.
appearance_lock.scale_lock: Length spans from an adult's wrist to just past the elbow when held; diameter is thin enough to be fully encircled by one hand. Never longer than a forearm-and-a-half, never a thick recorder-sized bore.
appearance_lock.negative_lock: No metal Irish tin-whistle sheen, no recorder mouthpiece block/fipple, no panpipe cluster of tubes, no bone or bamboo segmented look, no modern keyed woodwind mechanism, no bright lacquer, no ornate carving or runes, no case or strap attached in shot, no glowing or energy effects.

item_states.appearance: The plain honey-brown wooden flute as it exists throughout Kamin's lifetime on Kataan: unadorned, progressively hand-worn at the finger holes, held in a Kataanian villager's calloused hands. Silhouette and material never change across this state.

The identical flute, unchanged in design, now physically present in Picard's hands on the Enterprise bridge at the instant he wakes from the probe's neural link — the impossible object that crossed from the mental experience into physical reality.
The same unchanged flute kept afterward by Picard as a personal memento, seen resting on a small stand or being played alone in his quarters aboard the Enterprise-D.

canonical_facts.fact: A probe from the Kataan star system linked directly with Jean-Luc Picard's mind, causing him to experience an entire lifetime as a man named Kamin over roughly twenty-five minutes of real elapsed time.
Kataan's sun was dying and its people, unable to save their world or physically escape it, built and launched the probe generations earlier as their only means of being remembered.
As Kamin, Picard was taught to play the Ressikan flute by his friend and mentor Batai; it became Kamin's own instrument, played throughout his simulated life on Kataan.
Kamin married Eline, raised two children, and grew old across the simulated decades, continuing to play the flute through the years of worsening drought as Kataan's sun failed.

When Picard woke on the Enterprise bridge, no real time had passed except that he was inexplicably holding the actual wooden flute in his hands — an object the narrative does not fully explain crossing from the probe-induced experience into physical reality.
canonical_facts.status: television canon; the mechanism of the physical transfer is left unexplained in the episode

canonical_facts.fact: Picard kept the flute afterward as a personal keepsake and was later shown playing it alone, established across subsequent episodes as the only physical remnant of Kamin's entire lived life and the memory of the extinct Kataan civilization.
canonical_facts.status: television canon (established in The Inner Light; referenced again in later episodes such as TNG: Lessons)
canonical_facts.source: TNG: The Inner Light; TNG: Lessons

forbidden_claims: The flute is magical, glowing, or has any power beyond being a physical wooden object.
Picard's experience on Kataan was a shared telepathic illusion witnessed by the bridge crew; it was a private neural experience induced by the probe's beam.
The flute plays itself, moves on its own, or exhibits any sentience.
Any Kataan or Ressikan lore beyond what the episode itself establishes (no invented expanded-universe names, dates, or events).
Batai and Eline appear in any later live-action continuity beyond Picard's memory of them or verbal references.

items.canon_scope: Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan and Star Trek III: The Search for Spock canon — Project Genesis, Carol Marcus's team, Khan's seizure of Regula I, detonation in the Mutara Nebula, the Genesis Planet's formation and Spock's restoration, and the planet's later self-destruction / the Federation's ban on the technology.

appearance_lock.overall_shape: A titanium-gray briefcase-style housing with a carrying handle, side latch/dial, ventilation slots, and a circular viewport into the device's crystalline energy matrix. Starfleet delta insignia and a 'GENESIS' nameplate on the front panel.
appearance_lock.state_inert_device_matrix: Sealed, latch closed, control panel dim/steady amber, viewport showing a calm blue-green internal glow. Undamaged, no visible energy discharge.
appearance_lock.state_genesis_wave_detonation: Casing cracked with golden-white energy racing across it before being engulfed in an expanding detonation wave that reshapes the surrounding nebula into a new world. The device itself is destroyed/consumed in this state — only its effect (the forming/decaying planet, and a debris fragment) remains visible in later beats; the intact device box is never shown again after detonation.

items.voice_intent: measured Starfleet documentary lore narrator; calm scientific wonder for the origin beats shifting into grave restrained dread as the weapon's danger is revealed — one-off override of the series' default Klingon ceremonial war-narrator voice_policy, same precedent as the Ressikan Flute episode

recent_hooks: The first Klingon bat'leth turned Worf against Kor.
This is the Ressikan flute — proof Picard lived a stranger's entire lifetime in twenty-five real minutes.
A Federation science project built to create life, capable of ending it instead.
recent_fates: Transported into interstellar space after Worf and Kor concluded it would divide the Empire.
Kept by Picard as a private keepsake, the only physical trace of Kamin's lived life and the extinct Kataan civilization.
The Genesis Planet tore itself apart, and the Federation banned the technology as a doomsday weapon.

episode_summaries.arc: Mythic forging by Kahless, Hur'q theft, millennium-long disappearance, recovery by Worf, Kor, and Jadzia Dax, rivalry, and exile into space.
episode_summaries.narrative_mode_used: First-person pilot. Per user review, all future Item Story episodes use an external third-person lore narrator.

episode_summaries.arc: TNG 'The Inner Light': Kamin learns the flute from his mentor Batai, lives a full lifetime with Eline as Kataan's sun dies, watches the memory probe launch, and Picard wakes on the bridge with the flute already, impossibly, in his hands.
episode_summaries.narrative_mode_used: External third-person lore narration about the item, per the episode 1 correction — never first-person.
episode_summaries.notes: Lesson (shared with the same-session Genshin item-story episode): Scenarist's first monologue draft was 108 words for 6x5s=30s of picture, which would have rendered to roughly 55s at this bible's measured MiniMax rate — an ~83% overrun against the 40% masking cap in sound.md. Trimmed to 71 words before Sound ran (never generated at the bloated length), keeping the hook and all six canonical beats. Final TTS came in at 26.2s, an undershoot handled by Editor without leading silence. Also: this bible's series-level voice_policy/music_policy (dark ceremonial Klingon myth, war drums) is tonally wrong for a quiet Picard-memory item — Sound applied a one-off override (Elegant_Man voice, melancholy solo-flute music) for this episode. Worth revisiting whether voice_policy/music_policy should become per-item rather than series-wide before episode 3.

Fixed by regenerating scene-7 as a sealed archival records case (same Starfleet delta/GENESIS nameplate design lineage, no crystalline core, no energy cracks) rather than the active device. TTS also needed one re-render: first pass at speed 0.85 came back at 51.9s against a 35s window (48% mismatch, over item-story.md's 40% reject threshold) - re-rendered at speed 0.95 to reach 46.26s / 30% mismatch. Cost: Storyboarder ~$0.80 (2 refs + 7 scenes + 1 scene-7 regen), Sound ~$0.10, Animator $2.94 (7 clips, zero retries, zero content-policy hits).
